q: You must back up a server's configuration. Which folder matters most?
explain: Almost every setting of a Linux server lives as a text file under /etc: users, services, network, ssh. /bin only holds programs you can reinstall, /tmp is wiped, /proc is made up by the kernel. Changing data (logs, databases) is in /var: back it up too.

q: An app on your server starts failing and you don't know why. Where do you look first?
choices: Its config in /etc, to rewrite it
explain: The program usually writes why it fails: a missing file, a wrong setting, a port already taken. journalctl -u app shows the log of a service, /var/log holds the others. Read the error first: changing the config at random often adds a second problem.

q: Why work as your own user with sudo rather than logged in as root?
choices: Fewer accidents, and each sudo is logged with your name
explain: root can do anything, including breaking the system with one typo. With sudo you are only root for the one command you asked for, and the system logs who ran it. So mistakes are rarer, and you can find out later who changed what.

q: A server is slow. Which command shows what eats the CPU right now?
explain: top shows the running programs, refreshed every few seconds, the busiest first. Press M to sort by memory instead, q to quit (htop is a friendlier version). ps aux takes a single snapshot: handy in a script, less for watching.

q: How do you see who logged in to a server recently, and from where?
explain: last reads the record of past logins: who, from which address, when, and for how long. who only shows who is connected right now. A login from an address you don't know is worth a closer look.

q: Writes fail with 'No space left on device'. What do you check first?
explain: The message means a disk is full. df -h (disk free, in readable sizes) shows how full each disk is. free is about memory, not disk. Then du -sh /var/* shows which folder grew: often logs that nobody cleans.

q: free -h shows little 'free' memory but a lot 'available'. Is RAM short?
choices: No: spare RAM serves as cache and is given back
explain: Linux uses RAM nobody needs to keep recently read files, which makes the machine faster. That cache is handed back as soon as a program asks for memory. So look at 'available', not 'free': it is what programs can still get.

q: `ls -l` shows -rw-r--r-- on a file. Who can change it?
explain: After the first character (- for a file), read three blocks of rwx: owner, group, everyone else. r = read, w = write (change), x = run. Here only the owner has a w: rw-, then r--, r--. In numbers that is chmod 644.

q: A file with a database password is -rw-r--r--. What is wrong?
choices: Every user on the machine can read it
explain: The last r-- is for everyone else: any user or service on the machine can read the password. chmod 600 file keeps it to its owner only (rw-------). SSH even refuses to use a private key that others can read.

q: On a server, what is the file ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for?
choices: The public keys allowed to log in as you
explain: Each line is a public key. Whoever holds the matching private key can log in as you, without a password. Your private keys are elsewhere (~/.ssh/id_*), the servers you trust are in known_hosts. A line you don't recognise is an open door: remove it.

q: A process ignores Ctrl+C. What do you try before kill -9?
choices: kill PID, which lets it clean up
explain: kill PID politely asks the program to stop: it can save its work and close its files. kill -9 stops it at once, with no cleanup: half-written files, leftover lock files. Try kill first, wait a few seconds, and keep -9 for when it really won't stop.

q: You restart a web app and want to watch its log live. What do you run?
explain: tail -f (follow) prints the end of the file, then each new line as the app writes it. cat prints the file once and stops. Ctrl+C stops following. For a systemd service, journalctl -fu app does the same.

q: You change who may use sudo. Why edit with visudo?
choices: It checks the syntax: a typo could lock everyone out of sudo
explain: sudo reads /etc/sudoers on every call. If you save it with a typo, sudo refuses to work for everyone, and without a root password you are locked out. visudo edits a copy and checks the syntax before saving. Even safer: put your rule in a file of /etc/sudoers.d/ (visudo -f), and keep a root shell open while you test.

q: Someone may be trying to guess passwords on your server. Where do you see failed SSH logins?
choices: journalctl -u ssh, or the auth log in /var/log
explain: The SSH service logs every login attempt: journalctl -u ssh shows them, and so does /var/log/auth.log on Debian (/var/log/secure on Rocky). Hundreds of failures from one address mean a robot is guessing passwords. fail2ban blocks such addresses; allowing keys only removes the attack.

q: `ls -l` shows -rwsr-xr-x root on a program. What does the s mean?
choices: It runs as root, whoever starts it
explain: An s where the owner's x should be is the SUID bit: the program runs with its owner's rights, here root, whoever starts it. passwd needs it to write /etc/shadow. An SUID root program you don't recognise is a classic way to become root: find / -perm -4000 lists them all, to compare with a clean machine.

q: You added a disk to /etc/fstab. How do you test it before rebooting?
explain: /etc/fstab lists the disks to mount at boot. A wrong line can stop the machine at boot, which is painful on a remote server. mount -a mounts everything listed that isn't mounted yet, right now: a mistake shows up while you can still fix it. findmnt --verify checks the file without mounting.

q: `ss -tlnp` shows 0.0.0.0:5432 for postgres. What does it mean?
choices: It listens on every interface, reachable from outside
explain: The address before the port says where the program listens. 0.0.0.0 means every network interface, so any machine that can reach the server can try to connect to your database. 127.0.0.1 would mean this machine only. Make services listen only where needed, and let a firewall block the rest.

q: df -h shows free space, yet you get 'No space left on device'. What else can be full?
explain: A filesystem has two limits: space, and the number of files. Each file uses one inode, and their number is fixed when the disk is formatted. Millions of tiny files (sessions, cache, mail queues) can use them all while space remains. df -i shows inode use; find the folder with the most files and clean it.

q: You deleted a huge log, but df shows no space back. Why?
choices: A process still has it open
explain: rm removes the file's name, but while a program still has the file open, its data stays on disk. The service writing that log keeps it, and df sees no change. lsof +L1 lists deleted files still open; restarting that service frees the space. Next time, empty a log with > file (truncate) instead of rm.

q: ln creates links. What is the difference between a hard link and a soft (symbolic) link?
choices: A soft link points to a path, a hard link to the inode
explain: A soft link (ln -s) is a small file holding a path: delete or move the target and the link points to nothing. A hard link is a second name for the same data (the same inode): the data stays until the last name is removed. Hard links only work on the same disk; soft links go anywhere.

q: A script works by hand but fails from cron. Most likely cause?
choices: cron runs it with a tiny PATH and environment
explain: When you run a script by hand, it inherits your whole environment: your PATH, your variables, your current folder. cron starts it with almost nothing: a short PATH, no variables, from your home. Use full paths (/usr/local/bin/tool) or set PATH at the top of the crontab, and log the output with >> file 2>&1 to see the error.

q: A backup script logs in to a server by SSH. Which key should it use?
choices: Its own key, limited to that job in authorized_keys
root's key, copied to each server
One passphrase-less key shared by all scripts
explain: Give each automated job its own key. If it leaks, you revoke that one key without touching the others. In authorized_keys you can restrict it: command="…" allows only one command, from="…" only one source address. Your personal key, or a key shared everywhere, would give the script, and whoever steals it, far more than it needs.

q: Despite its name, /etc/passwd holds no password today. What is it for?
choices: The list of accounts: name, id, home and shell
The list of groups on the machine
The list of users logged in right now
explain: It lists the accounts: one line per user, name:x:uid:gid:comment:home:shell. Programs read it to turn a user id into a name, which is why everyone can read it. The x means the password is elsewhere, in /etc/shadow. A second account with uid 0 is a second root: always suspicious.

q: Where are the password hashes kept on a modern Linux?
explain: The system doesn't store passwords but hashes: a fingerprint computed from the password that can't be turned back into it. They are in /etc/shadow, readable by root only, since a stolen hash can still be attacked offline by guessing. That's why /etc/passwd, which holds none, can stay readable by all.

q: In /etc/shadow, which second field means the account has a usable password?
explain: A value starting with $ is a hash: the letters between the first two $ name the method. $y$ is yescrypt (today's default), $6$ SHA-512, $2b$ bcrypt. ! or * in that field block password login (the account may still use SSH keys), and an empty field means no password at all: dangerous.

q: You edited sshd_config on a remote server. What do you do before reloading sshd?
choices: sshd -t, and keep your current session open
explain: sshd -t reads the config and reports any error without touching the running service. Even with a valid file, a wrong setting can refuse your login. So reload, keep your current session open (it stays connected), and try a new login from another terminal. Only close the old one when the new one works.

q: A process with a random name runs from /tmp. What do you do first?
choices: Note its binary and connections before killing it
explain: A program with a random name running from /tmp is typical of an intrusion (a crypto miner, a backdoor). If you kill it first, you lose what it could teach you. ls -l /proc/PID/exe shows its file, ss -tnp its network connections: note them. Then cut the machine off the network and investigate how it got in.

q: Which sshd setting stops password guessing altogether?
explain: With PasswordAuthentication no, sshd accepts only keys, so there's no password left to guess and the robots fail every time. Moving to port 2222 only reduces the noise in the logs; the attack still works. Before switching, check in another session that your key login works, or you lock yourself out.

q: You log in to a new server. What does `sudo -l` tell you?
choices: The commands you may run with sudo
The users in the sudo group
explain: sudo -l lists what your account may run with sudo on this machine, and whether it needs a password. Attackers run it first too: a line like (ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim is root for anyone, because vim can start a shell (:!sh). Allow full commands with care, never editors or shells.

q: Services keep PID files and sockets in /run. What kind of folder is /run?
choices: Runtime files, in memory, emptied at each boot
explain: /run lives in memory (tmpfs) and is emptied at each boot. Running programs keep there what only matters while they run: their PID file, their socket, lock files. So nothing there survives a reboot, and nothing there should be backed up. /var/run is only a link to it.

q: You build a tool from source on a server. Why install it under /usr/local and not /usr?
choices: Software you installed outside the package manager
Local copies of the package cache
explain: The package manager owns /usr: it may overwrite or remove files there at the next upgrade, and it doesn't know about yours. /usr/local is left to the admin for software installed by hand. make install uses /usr/local by default, and it comes first in PATH.

q: Why send a server's logs to another machine as well?
choices: An intruder who gets root can erase the local ones
Logs are faster to write there
explain: The first thing an intruder who becomes root does is erase their traces in the local logs. A copy sent live to another machine, which they can't reach, stays intact. rsyslog or systemd-journal-upload do the sending. After an incident, that remote copy is the one you trust.

q: You run gpg -c notes.txt and type a passphrase. What do you have now?
choices: notes.txt.gpg, and notes.txt still in clear
explain: gpg -c writes a locked copy, notes.txt.gpg, and leaves the original untouched. Until you delete notes.txt, the secret is still readable on the disk. Check the .gpg opens (gpg -d notes.txt.gpg), then remove the clear file.

q: Why keep passwords in pass instead of a passwords.txt file?
choices: Each one is encrypted with your gpg key
pass files are hidden from ls
explain: pass stores each password in its own file, encrypted with your gpg key: a copied disk or a backup shows nothing without your private key. A text file, even with chmod 600, is readable by root, by any program you run, and in every backup.

q: A script starts with DB_PASSWORD="s3cret". What is the real problem?
choices: Whoever reads the script, or its git history, has it
explain: A password written in a script travels with it: into git, backups, screenshots, a colleague's copy. Fetch it when the script runs instead: DB_PASSWORD="$(pass show db/prod)". A password that was ever committed must be changed, since the history keeps it.

q: A project gives tool.tar.gz, tool.tar.gz.sig and its public key. What does gpgv tell you?
choices: Who signed it, and that nothing changed since
That the file has no virus
That the key is not expired only
explain: A signature is made with the project's private key; its public key checks it. Good signature: the file comes from whoever holds that key and wasn't changed. It says nothing about viruses, and it's only worth something if you got the right public key, from the project's site.

q: You encrypt a file for a colleague with gpg -e -r colleague. Who can open it?
choices: Only the colleague, with their private key
Anyone with the colleague's public key
You and the colleague both, always
explain: -e encrypts for a public key: only the matching private key opens it. Their public key can lock files for them, never unlock them. Even you can't open it again unless you also add yourself with a second -r.

q: pass init asks for a gpg key id. Why does the store need your key?
choices: Every password is encrypted for that key
To log in to a server
explain: pass encrypts every password it stores for the key(s) listed in ~/.password-store/.gpg-id, and decrypts with your private key when you run pass show. Lose the private key and the passwords are gone: keep a backup of it (gpg --export-secret-keys) somewhere safe and offline.
